outcome: Since 26 January 2024 one new event bears on the problem: an LLM-assisted preprint (arXiv 2601.22365, 29 January 2026; ICML 2026 poster) certifies a lower bound of 0.8559 on the planar Steiner ratio, short of the conjectured sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866, which the authors say remains open; the 1990/1992 Du-Hwang claimed proof of the equality stays disputed, and no source found establishes it.
problem_asks: (1) For every finite set P of points in the Euclidean plane, the Steiner minimum tree length Ls(P) is at least (sqrt(3)/2) times Lm(P), where Lm(P) is the length of the Euclidean minimum spanning tree of P (the Gilbert-Pollak inequality). (2) The constant sqrt(3)/2 is the Steiner ratio, i.e. the infimum of Ls(P)/Lm(P) over finite planar P is exactly sqrt(3)/2 and not smaller. The equilateral triangle with unit side gives Ls = sqrt(3), Lm = 2, ratio sqrt(3)/2 exactly, so the attainment half of (2) is elementary; the content lies in (1), which is what makes the infimum equal the constant. Convention: the Wikipedia article defines the ratio as the supremum of Lm/Ls, which is 2/sqrt(3); the bullet uses the Ls/Lm = sqrt(3)/2 form. Both are the same claim.

events.what_happened: Ding-Zhu Du and Frank K. Hwang, 'A new bound for the Steiner ratio', Transactions of the AMS 278(1) (1983), pp. 137-148. Per the AMS record (search snippet, not opened) they prove the ratio is greater than 0.8. This is an earlier step in the lower-bound sequence 0.577 (Graham-Hwang 1976), 0.743 (Chung-Hwang 1978), 0.8 (Du-Hwang 1983), 0.824 (Chung-Graham 1985).
events.delivers: Lower bound: Ls(P) >= 0.8 Lm(P) for all finite planar P. A bound on the named quantity, with constant 0.8 below sqrt(3)/2.
events.remains: The sharp constant sqrt(3)/2 and therefore the full inequality (1) with sqrt(3)/2; all of (2) beyond 0.8.

checked_by.who: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society (referee process)

events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture: a lower bound on the ratio. Consistent with, and weaker than, sqrt(3)/2.

events.what_happened: F. R. K. Chung and R. L. Graham, 'A new bound for Euclidean Steiner minimal trees', Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 440 (1985), pp. 328-346 (Discrete Geometry and Convexity). Gives the lower bound 0.824168..., described in a 2024 arXiv paper (secondary) as the unique root in (0.8, 1) of a degree-12 polynomial. The 2026 Ke et al. paper calls this the previous state of the art and says no later improvement was reported for about four decades. The 2025 Teplitskaya survey instead gives 0.842 (1985) as the best proven bound, citing [11] (Chung-Graham). The conflict is unresolved; the original paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound: Ls(P) >= 0.824... Lm(P) for all finite planar P (per secondary sources). A bound on the named quantity.
events.remains: The gap from 0.824 to sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866; equality in (1); all of (2) beyond 0.824.

checked_by.who: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences (proceedings volume, Discrete Geometry and Convexity)

events.doubts: The value is inconsistent across sources: 0.824 (Ke et al. 2026; 2024 arXiv snippet) versus 0.842 (Teplitskaya 2025 survey; an Algorithmica L_p abstract snippet also reports 0.842 for Chung-Graham). Not resolved here.
events.direction: Partial result in the direction of the conjecture (a lower bound).

events.what_happened: D.-Z. Du, E. Yao, F. K. Hwang, 'The Steiner ratio conjecture is true for five points', Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series A (1985). Title seen in a ScienceDirect search result; the paper itself was not opened. Cited in the 2026 Ke et al. reference list.
events.delivers: Proves the conjecture (1) for every finite planar P with at most five points. A restricted case by number of points.
events.remains: Inequality (1) for six or more points; the general case (2) for all finite P.

events.what_happened: Du and Hwang claim the full conjecture. Public written forms: (a) 'The Steiner ratio conjecture of Gilbert and Pollak is true', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 87(23) (December 1990), pp. 9464-9466, DOI 10.1073/pnas.87.23.9464, PMCID PMC55186 - an abridged proof per its abstract (abstract text from search snippet; the PMC page returned a CAPTCHA and was not opened); (b) an extended abstract 'An approach for proving lower bounds: solution of Gilbert-Pollak's conjecture on Steiner ratio', Proc. 31st IEEE FOCS (1990), pp. 76-85 (cited in a reference list seen in a search snippet; not opened); (c) full version 'A proof of the Gilbert-Pollak conjecture on the Steiner ratio', Algorithmica 7 (1992), pp. 121-135, DOI 10.1007/BF01758755 (Springer redirected to a login page; not opened). Date given as 1990 because the FOCS and PNAS forms are both 1990 and the earliest month was not pinned down.
events.revisions: PNAS abridged (Dec 1990); FOCS extended abstract (1990); Algorithmica full version (1992). No erratum or withdrawal found. Ivanov-Tuzhilin (2012) say Du and Hwang published claimed proofs in 1990 and 1992.
events.delivers: As claimed: for every finite planar P, Ls(P) >= (sqrt(3)/2) Lm(P), which is the full inequality (1) and therefore the sharp constant (2). The abstract as seen in a snippet states the inequality for any finite P with the equilateral triangle as the lower-bound example; no restriction to point count or dimension is stated there. Per the later critiques (Innami et al. 2010; de Wet 2008/09; Ivanov-Tuzhilin 2011/2012/2014) the key lemma is not established, so the delivered result is disputed.
events.remains: As claimed: nothing. On the critiques' reading: the general inequality (1), hence (2), is not established; the critics report that the 7-point case survives (de Wet) and that the method works only for small point counts.

events.doubts: (a) Innami et al. 2010 (Algorithmica 57, 869-872): evidence against continuity of minimum inner spanning tree length with respect to a parameter vector having a zero component, stated as the key step of the Du-Hwang proof; they conclude the conjecture is not proved. (b) de Wet thesis (submitted 31 January 2008; cited as 2009): 'a fundamental gap in the proof of Du and Hwang', with counterexamples to a claim about inner spanning trees; the thesis says the general question 'seems once again to be an open question' (abstract as summarised). (c) Ivanov and Tuzhilin (Algorithmica 2012; arXiv 1402.6079, 2014): the gaps are traced to the 'characteristic area' of a minimal Steiner tree, which was introduced informally; attempts to formalise it fail because the required properties contradict one another; a monotonicity property needed for reduction to full Steiner minimal trees is involved. (d) Wu and Zhong (2011) revisit the same method and, per Ivanov-Tuzhilin, repeat the mistake; they checked monotonicity only on a 5-gon example (not opened). (e) Wikipedia (Ding-Zhu Du biography, as fetched): 'The proof of the Gilbert-Pollak conjecture was later found to have gaps, leaving the problem unsolved.' (f) Rubinstein and Weng (1997) derive a sphere result from the planar claim; Innami et al. note that conditionality. No published defence of the Du-Hwang argument was found.
events.direction: Claims the sharp inequality, i.e. agrees with the conjecture's assertion. Critiques say the argument fails at a key lemma, and the status is therefore unsettled.

Cited in the 2026 Ke et al. reference list and by secondary sources; not opened. Secondary sources say it used a variational / configuration-space method.
events.delivers: Proves the conjecture (1) for every finite planar P with at most six points. A restricted case by number of points.
events.remains: Inequality (1) for seven or more points; the general case (2).

events.what_happened: Yana Teplitskaya, 'Open problems on Steiner trees and maximal distance minimizers', arXiv 2511.18217 (math.MG), submitted 22 November 2025. States that the planar Steiner ratio conjecture 'is still open (as of 2025 year)', citing Ivanov-Tuzhilin 2012; calls it 'the most well-known open problem on Steiner tree'; gives Graham's offered prize; gives the best proven planar bound as about 0.842 (1985, Chung-Graham). Read via a summarising fetch of the HTML version.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 (22 Nov 2025). Metadata version only.
events.delivers: No new result. A status statement: the planar conjecture is open as of 2025; a survey of the bounds.
events.doubts: The survey's 0.842 figure disagrees with the 0.824 cited in the 2026 Ke et al. paper; not resolved here.
events.direction: Status statement: the conjecture is open; no bearing on the value.

events.what_happened: Yisi Ke, Tianyu Huang, Yankai Shu, Di He, Jingchu Gai, Liwei Wang, 'Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via Large Language Models', arXiv 2601.22365 (cs.DM, cs.LG; equal contribution and co-corresponding authors noted; Peking University affiliation per secondary sources; Carnegie Mellon also appears in one secondary summary). The abstract presents 'a novel AI system for obtaining tighter lower bounds on the Steiner ratio'. Rather than asking LLMs to prove the conjecture, the authors task them with generating rule-constrained geometric lemmas implemented as executable code; these become 'verification functions' that yield certified lower bounds. Through progressive, reflection-driven lemma refinement the system establishes a certified lower bound of 0.8559. The paper describes the conjecture as open. Accepted as an ICML 2026 poster (Seoul, session 7 July 2026, per the ICML page). Repository: github.com/keyisi2006/Steiner-Ratio.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2026; v2 21 May 2026 (arXiv comment '44 pages, 11 figures'); v3 2 Sep 2026 (current). Both v1 and v3 extractions give the same 0.8559 bound and the same AI disclosure sentences. I could not determine what changed between versions beyond the bound's value being stated in each.
events.delivers: A certified lower bound: the Steiner ratio of the Euclidean plane (inf of Ls/Lm over finite planar sets) is at least 0.8559. Restrictions visible in the repository and in extracts of the paper: the certificate is organised as two cases, d_regular and d_steiner, each with subcases f >= d and f <= d (README); the README says verification is performed 'only at the boundary f = d rather than checking the entire box', and a table lists n = 5 to 8 (meaning not explained in what I read). An extract of the paper says the 4-point lemmas are proven only at f = d and that Appendix C excludes some high-complexity 4-point lemmas in Cases 1 and 3; another extract says symbolic verification was not performed for variable ff. Whether the 0.8559 bound holds for all finite planar sets without these restrictions is not established by what I could read. It improves the quoted previous lower bound 0.824 (Chung-Graham 1985).
events.remains: Equality in (1) and the exact value sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866 in (2): the gap from 0.8559 to 0.8660 is open, and the paper says the conjecture remains open.

events.directly_checkable: Partly: the certificate directory holds d_regular/ and d_steiner/ with splits, lemmas and verification scripts (per README). I did not run them. The README says verification is only at the boundary f = d, so a reader must decide whether that suffices.
events.doubts: (a) Scope of verification: the README says verification is only at f = d 'rather than checking the entire box'. One extraction of arXiv v1 HTML reported the sentence 'this bound has been rigorously verified across the entire parameter space'; a second extraction of the same HTML did not find that phrase, and the first extraction's exact wording could not be re-located. (b) Authors' own admissions of partial verification in extracts: 4-point lemmas proven only at f = d; Appendix C excludes high-complexity 4-point lemmas in Cases 1 and 3; symbolic verification not performed for variable ff. (c) Internal inconsistency in the iteration count: 'about ten iterations' in the introduction and 'roughly a dozen iterative rounds' in results (per extract). (d) Human checks are the authors' own; no named independent expert reading or critique found in searches run through 13 October 2026. (e) The Machine Heart description (reward model, divide-and-conquer, 'verified by human experts') does not appear in the arXiv extracts. (f) No formal proof-assistant certificate. (g) Lower bound only; it does not touch the equality, so it does not by itself settle any part of problem_asks beyond the bound.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture only on the lower-bound side: 0.8559 is consistent with sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866 and does not contradict it. The equality is not moved.
events.object: No point configuration is exhibited. The exhibited item is a computer-assisted certificate: a family of LLM-proposed geometric lemmas implemented as code ('verification functions'), which, checked by the repository's scripts and by Mathematica computations (per the paper), certify rho >= 0.8559 on the stated cases. Not a non-constructive existence proof; the certificate is computational and, per the README, checked on the boundary f = d.

The paper says LLMs generate rule-constrained geometric lemmas implemented as executable code, which become verification functions yielding the certified bound (abstract and ICML page). The sources do not say which model proposed which lemma, nor whether GPT-5 contributed to the final certified bound directly. The authors also say 'the LLM acts solely as a reasoning engine, offloading all validation tasks to Mathematica', so Mathematica does the checking, not the AI system.

disputes.summary: Du and Hwang (PNAS 1990 abridged; Algorithmica 1992 full) claim the sharp inequality. Critics report gaps: Innami et al. (Algorithmica 2010), de Wet (Unisa 2008/2009), Ivanov and Tuzhilin (Algorithmica 2012; arXiv 2014); Wikipedia's Du biography says the proof 'was later found to have gaps, leaving the problem unsolved'. Older sources still present it as proved: the DIMACS achievements page (search snippet) and an Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry (search snippet); a 2011 arXiv paper on manifolds treats the planar result as established. The 2025 survey and the 2026 Ke et al. paper call the conjecture open. No published defence of the Du-Hwang argument was found.

The best earlier lower bound is given as 0.824 (Chung-Graham 1985) in the 2026 Ke et al. paper and in 2024-era snippets, but as about 0.842 (1985) in the 2025 Teplitskaya survey, which cites Chung-Graham. A snippet of an Algorithmica L_p Steiner-tree abstract also reports 0.842 for Chung-Graham. Not resolved; the original Chung-Graham paper was not opened.

The 2026 paper's own statements about verification conflict in the extracts: one extract reports 'rigorously verified across the entire parameter space'; the repository README describes checking only at the boundary f = d 'rather than checking the entire box', and another extract reports 4-point lemmas proven only at f = d with some high-complexity cases excluded. Whether the 0.8559 bound is unrestricted is disputed between the paper's sentence and its repository.

Machine Heart (secondary, 18 May 2026) credits a Peking University team with a reward model and divide-and-conquer framework and says human experts verified the result. The arXiv extracts I read do not mention a reward model or divide-and-conquer, and the ICML page lists authors that one secondary summary places at Peking University and Carnegie Mellon. Not resolved; the Machine Heart original was not opened.

summary:
The problem is the Gilbert-Pollak (planar Steiner ratio) inequality Ls(P) >= (sqrt(3)/2) Lm(P). Its only published full claim is Du and Hwang's: an abridged proof in PNAS (December 1990, 'The Steiner ratio conjecture of Gilbert and Pollak is true') and a full version in Algorithmica (1992). I could not read either directly (the PNAS page returned a CAPTCHA and the Springer page redirected to a login); their content rests on search snippets and on the critics' descriptions. Critiques followed. Innami, Kim, Mashiko and Shiohama (Algorithmica 2010) offered evidence against the continuity of minimum inner spanning tree length at a zero parameter component, which they say is the key step. de Wet's Unisa thesis (repository date 31 January 2008) reports a fundamental gap with counterexamples to an inner-spanning-tree claim, and proves the case of seven or fewer points, while stating that the general question 'seems once again to be an open question'. Ivanov and Tuzhilin (Algorithmica 2012, 'Still Open'; arXiv 1402.6079, 2014) trace the trouble to the informally introduced 'characteristic area' of a minimal Steiner tree; Wu and Zhong (2011) are said to repeat the mistake. Wikipedia's Du biography says the proof 'was later found to have gaps, leaving the problem unsolved', and the Gilbert-Pollak article (last edit 18 April 2026, per footer as fetched) calls the conjecture unproven. Restricted cases: five points (Du, Yao, Hwang 1985), six points (Rubinstein and Thomas 1991), seven or fewer (de Wet). Some older sources still say proved (DIMACS achievements page; an Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry, both via snippets), and a 2011 manifolds paper treats the planar result as established, which the later critiques contradict. The Rubinstein-Weng 1997 sphere result rests on the planar claim.

In the window (after 26 January 2024), the only new event is the 2026 LLM-assisted certified lower bound: Ke, Huang, Shu, He, Gai and Wang, arXiv 2601.22365 (submitted 29 January 2026; v2 21 May; v3 2 September 2026), an ICML 2026 poster. It certifies Steiner ratio >= 0.8559, improving the quoted 0.824 (Chung-Graham 1985), by having LLMs propose rule-constrained geometric lemmas as executable code that become 'verification functions', checked with Mathematica and repository scripts. This is AI-involved in a load-bearing way per the authors' own account: they name GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Pro as the models used in their experiments. The lower bound is consistent with sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866 and does not contradict it, but it does not settle the equality. Human checking is the authors' own (every lemma manually checked; independent manual verification of generated proofs), plus an ICML poster acceptance and a secondary press account that human experts verified it. I found no named independent expert reading, critique or follow-up improvement through 13 October 2026, about 8.5 months after posting. Doubts from the paper and repository: the README says verification is only at the boundary f = d 'rather than checking the entire box', an extract of the paper contains 'rigorously verified across the entire parameter space' which a second extraction did not find, 4-point lemmas are proven only at f = d with some high-complexity cases excluded, and the iteration count is given two ways. The repository's Machine Heart-reported reward model and divide-and-conquer approach do not appear in the arXiv text I read. No Lean or Coq formalisation was found.

Where a call was close: (i) whether the 2026 event 'moves a quantity the problem names' (it moves the lower bound on the Steiner ratio, which the statement names) or merely checks instances (the bound is a single certified number over a stated set of cases) depends on whether the certificate is unrestricted, which the sources leave unclear; (ii) whether the 1990-92 claim counts as a resolution (it would, if accepted, and then the 2026 result would be a bound on a settled constant), which the 2008-2014 critiques and the 2025/2026 status sources contest; (iii) the 0.824 versus 0.842 discrepancy for the prior record does not change the direction of the 2026 result, but affects how much it is said to move the bound.
competing_reading: Accepting the refereed Algorithmica 1992 proof (and treating the 2008-2014 critiques as incomplete, as the DIMACS page and the 2011 manifolds paper imply) would make the planar inequality, and so the sharp constant, a 1992 theorem. On that reading the problem is solved decades before the window, and the 2026 LLM result is a bound on an already-known constant. Conversely, reading the 2026 certificate as unrestricted (the 'entire parameter space' sentence, and 'rigorously certified' in the README) would make it a genuine machine-assisted quantitative advance on a bound the problem names, despite leaving the equality open. Reading the README's boundary-only check and the partial 4-point lemmas as limits makes it a computer-assisted bound on a restricted set of configurations.
what_would_settle_it: (a) For the 1990-92 claim: the Algorithmica 1992 text and the 1990 FOCS and PNAS texts, read against Innami et al. (2010) and the de Wet thesis (inner spanning tree counterexamples), and against any published reply to Ivanov-Tuzhilin (2012, 2014). (b) For the 2026 event: the full arXiv v3 PDF (its appendix lemmas and the 'entire parameter space' sentence), the GitHub certificate scripts run on the stated cases and the boundary-versus-box question answered, an independent expert's written check, and the ICML OpenReview record of referee comments. (c) For the prior bound: the original Chung-Graham 1985 paper, to settle 0.824 versus 0.842. (d) For the AI attribution: the authors' statement of which model generated which lemma and whether GPT-5 or Gemini 3 Pro contributed to the final certified inequalities.
